answer.question: My mom just turned 65 and is signing up for Medicare. How much will her Part B premium be each month in 2026, and is there anything that could make it higher?
answer.answer:
In 2026 the standard Part B premium is $202.90 a month, and most people pay that amount. Two things can make it higher:

1. Income. Medicare uses the modified adjusted gross income reported on your IRS tax return from 2 years ago to set the premium, so a higher income can mean a higher monthly amount.
2. A late enrollment penalty. If she doesn't sign up for Part B when she's first eligible, her monthly premium may go up 10% for each full 12-month period she could have had Part B but didn't sign up, and she'd pay that penalty for as long as she has Part B. (Signing up during a Special Enrollment Period, or enrolling in a Medicare Savings Program, may mean no penalty.)

Since she just turned 65, her Initial Enrollment Period is the 7-month period that begins 3 months before the month she turns 65 and ends 3 months after — signing up then avoids the penalty. If she gets Social Security or Railroad Retirement Board benefits, the premium is deducted from her monthly benefit payment.

answer.question: Dad has Original Medicare and no other insurance. He spent 5 days in the hospital and then went straight into a skilled nursing facility for 30 days. What will he owe for that in 2026?
answer.answer: The excerpts here don't give the 2026 dollar amounts, so I can't total his costs. What they do say: Medicare Part A covers short-term skilled nursing facility (SNF) care after a 3-day minimum medically necessary inpatient hospital stay for an illness or injury related to that stay, so his 5-day stay meets the 3-day requirement. A "benefit period" is how Original Medicare measures hospital and SNF use — it begins the day he's admitted as an inpatient and ends when he's had no inpatient hospital or skilled care for 60 days in a row, and he must pay the inpatient hospital deductible for each benefit period. Because the hospital stay and SNF stay run together, they fall in the same benefit period, so he'd pay one inpatient hospital deductible. With Original Medicare and no other coverage (like Medigap, Medicaid, or employer/retiree coverage), there's no limit on what he pays out of pocket in a year. For the exact 2026 deductible and the daily SNF coinsurance amounts, call 1-800-MEDICARE (TTY 1-877-486-2048), visit Medicare.gov, or contact your State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) — you can find your local SHIP at shiphelp.org.

answer.answer: Medicare pays first in your situation. answer.question: My mom turns 65 on March 12. When can she sign up for Medicare without paying a penalty, and when would her coverage start?
answer.answer:
Because her birthday is March 12 (not the first of the month), her Initial Enrollment Period is the 7-month window that starts 3 months before the month she turns 65 and ends 3 months after — so December through June, with March being her birthday month. Signing up during that period avoids a late enrollment penalty.

When coverage starts depends on when she signs up:
- If she signs up during the first 3 months of the period (December, January, or February), her coverage begins the first day of her birthday month — March 1.
- If she signs up in March (the month she turns 65) or during the last 3 months (April, May, or June), her coverage starts the first day of the month after she signs up.

Note: separately, for Medicare drug coverage (Part D), she may owe a late enrollment penalty if she enrolls after her Initial Enrollment Period ends and goes 63 or more days in a row without Medicare drug coverage or other creditable prescription drug coverage.

If you sign up the month you turn 65 or during the last 3 months of your Initial Enrollment Period, your coverage starts the first day of the month after you sign up.

You may have to pay a late enrollment penalty if you enroll at any time after your Initial Enrollment Period is over and there’s a period of 63 or more days in a row when you don’t have Medicare drug coverage or other creditable prescription drug coverage.

answer.question: My husband is retiring in April and I'm 67 and covered by his employer's health plan. How long will I have to sign up for Part B, and does taking COBRA buy me more time?
answer.answer: After the coverage based on your husband's current employment ends, you have 8 months to sign up for Part B without a late enrollment penalty — and that 8 months runs whether or not you choose COBRA. COBRA does not extend it: COBRA coverage isn't considered coverage based on current employment, so it doesn't count as current employer coverage for this Special Enrollment Period, and you generally aren't eligible for a Special Enrollment Period when the COBRA coverage ends. The handbook also warns that if you have COBRA and you're eligible for Medicare, COBRA may only pay a small portion of your medical costs, so there may be reasons to take Part B instead of, or in addition to, COBRA. If you delay past that window, your monthly Part B premium may go up 10% for each full 12 months you could have had Part B but didn't sign up, for as long as you have Part B. To sign up, visit SSA.gov/medicare/sign-up.

answer.question: My mother found a Medicare Advantage plan with a $0 monthly premium. Does that mean she would pay nothing each month for her Medicare?
answer.answer: No — a $0 plan premium doesn't mean $0 each month. Even with a $0 Medicare Advantage premium, your mother still usually pays the monthly Part B (Medical Insurance) premium, and the Part A premium too if she doesn't have premium-free Part A. Some Medicare Advantage plans do help pay all or part of the Part B premium (sometimes called a "Medicare Part B premium reduction"), so it's worth checking whether her plan does that. Also keep in mind that a $0 premium doesn't mean $0 care costs — out-of-pocket costs like copayments and deductibles vary by plan, and she can't use Medigap to pay a Medicare Advantage plan's copayments, deductibles, or premiums.

answer.question: When is the best time for my dad to buy a Medigap policy, and what happens if he waits?
answer.answer: The best time is during his Medigap Open Enrollment Period — a 6-month period that starts the first month he has Medicare Part B (Medical Insurance) and is 65 or older. (Some states have additional Open Enrollment Periods.) If he waits until after that period, he may not be able to buy a Medigap policy at all, or it may cost more. In certain situations he may still have "guaranteed issue rights" — a right to buy a Medigap policy outside that period. Note also that if he delays signing up for Part B because he has group health coverage based on his (or his spouse's) current employment, his Medigap Open Enrollment Period won't start until he gets Part B. To learn more about his rights to buy a policy, he can call his State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) (phone numbers on pages 114–117) or his State Insurance Department; he can also compare policies and pricing at Medicare.gov/medigap-supplemental-insurance-plans.

answer.question: Mom's cancer is terminal and her doctor brought up hospice. Who has to sign off before Medicare will cover it, and what would she have to pay?
answer.answer:
The excerpt on hospice explains the costs but not the certification requirement. On costs, with Medicare-certified hospice care you pay: nothing for hospice care; a copayment of up to $5 per prescription for outpatient drugs for pain and symptom management; and 5% of the Medicare-approved amount for inpatient respite care (care in a Medicare-approved facility so a caregiver can rest, for up to 5 days each time). Medicare won't pay room and board in a facility where she lives, unless the hospice medical team decides she needs short-term inpatient care to manage pain and other symptoms, and Original Medicare still pays for covered benefits for health problems unrelated to the terminal illness.

As for who must sign off before Medicare covers hospice, these excerpts don't say. For that, check Medicare.gov/coverage or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227); TTY users can call 1-877-486-2048.

answer.question: My parents have Original Medicare. They're going to Portugal in June and to Puerto Rico in October. Would Medicare cover them if one of them ended up in the hospital on either trip?
answer.answer:
The two trips are different. Portugal is outside the U.S., and with Original Medicare "Original Medicare generally doesn’t cover medical care outside the U.S." They may be able to buy a Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap) policy that covers emergency care outside the U.S.

Puerto Rico is part of the U.S., so Original Medicare works there: with Original Medicare you can go to any Medicare-enrolled doctor, other health care provider, hospital, or other facility that accepts Medicare patients anywhere in the U.S. They'd still pay their usual share of the cost for covered services, and there's no limit to what they'll pay out of pocket in a year unless they have other coverage (like Medigap, Medicaid, employer, retiree, or union coverage). They should bring their red, white, and blue Medicare card.

The excerpts don't specifically name Puerto Rico, so for confirmation about that trip or about buying a Medigap policy for travel abroad, they can call 1-800-MEDICARE (TTY 1-877-486-2048) or contact their State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) at shiphelp.org.

answer.question: Mom spent three nights in the hospital but the billing office says she was under observation the whole time, never admitted. She needs a skilled nursing facility now. Will Part A pay for it?
answer.answer:
Probably not, based on the rule the handbook gives. Medicare covers short-term skilled nursing facility (SNF) care only after a 3-day minimum medically necessary **inpatient** hospital stay (not counting the day she leaves) for an illness or injury related to that stay. You're an inpatient only when the hospital formally admits you with a doctor's order; if you're getting observation services you're an outpatient, even if you spend the night in the hospital. So observation nights don't count toward the 3 days.

Two exceptions the handbook mentions: she may not need the 3-day inpatient stay if her doctor participates in an Accountable Care Organization (ACO) approved for a Skilled Nursing Facility 3-Day Rule Waiver — ask the provider — and Medicare Advantage Plans may also waive the 3-day minimum, so contact the plan.

Also worth knowing: if she was under observation more than 24 hours, the hospital must give her a "Medicare Outpatient Observation Notice" ("MOON") explaining why she's an outpatient and how it affects what she pays for care after she leaves. You now have appeal rights when a hospital changes your status from inpatient to outpatient if you meet certain conditions — see Medicare.gov/providers-services/claims-appeals-complaints/appeals/original-medicare. For more on benefit periods, visit Medicare.gov/coverage/skilled-nursing-facility-care.

answer.question: My father moved to the U.S. at 58 and has only about 6 years of work here. Does he have to pay for Part A, how much in 2026, and what happens if he puts it off?
answer.answer:
If he didn't work (or a spouse didn't work) long enough paying Medicare taxes to get "premium-free Part A," he may be able to buy Part A instead. In 2026 the Part A premium is either $311 or $565 each month, depending on how long he or his spouse worked and paid Medicare taxes. The handbook doesn't say how many years of work puts someone at each amount, so check with Medicare — visit Medicare.gov or call 1-800-MEDICARE.

If he puts it off: if he isn't eligible for premium-free Part A and doesn't buy it when he's first eligible, his monthly premium may go up 10%, and he'll pay that higher premium for twice the number of years he could have had Part A but didn't sign up (for example, 2 years without signing up means 4 years of the 10% higher premium).

Two other things to know: in most cases, if he chooses to buy Part A he must also have Part B and pay monthly premiums for both (the standard Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90); if he chooses not to buy Part A, he can still buy Part B if he's eligible. If he needs help paying the Part A premium, see pages 91–92 of the handbook.

answer.question: Mom's only income is her Social Security check and she's struggling to pay her Medicare premiums. Is there a program that would help, and would it do anything for her drug costs?
answer.answer:
Yes — the handbook describes two kinds of help, and the excerpts show they're connected.

- **Medicare Savings Programs** are state programs that "help with other Medicare costs" (such as premiums).
- **Extra Help** is the program for Medicare drug coverage (Part D) costs. Some people qualify automatically; if she didn't, "you can apply any time at SSA.gov/extrahelp."

A useful shortcut: when she applies for Extra Help, she "can also begin the application process for a Medicare Savings Program" — Social Security will send information to the state to start that application unless she tells them not to on the Extra Help form. Qualifying for Extra Help also means she won't owe a late enrollment penalty if she joins a drug plan later.

The excerpts don't list the income or resource limits for either program. For help with Extra Help questions or choosing drug coverage, she can call her State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) — phone numbers are on pages 114–117 of the handbook, or visit shiphelp.org — or call 1-800-MEDICARE (TTY 1-877-486-2048).

answer.question: Mom is in a Medicare Advantage plan and wants to move to a different one for next year. When can she make that change, and when would the new plan kick in?
answer.answer:
She has two main chances:

1. Open Enrollment Period in the fall — if the plan gets her enrollment request by December 7, her new coverage starts January 1.

2. Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, January 1 to March 31 — if she's already in a Medicare Advantage Plan, she can switch to another Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage) during this period. She can only make one change during this period, and the change takes effect the first of the month after the plan gets her request.

There's also a 5-star Special Enrollment Period (December 8 to November 30 the following year) if a plan with a 5-star quality rating is available in her area, and she may qualify for a Special Enrollment Period if something like a move or loss of other coverage happens. Otherwise, in most cases she must keep the plan she joins for the calendar year.

answer.question: Mom joined a Medicare Advantage plan in January and already regrets it. It's now February. Can she move to a different plan, and how many times can she change?
answer.answer: Yes. February falls within the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, which runs January 1 to March 31. During this period, if she's in a Medicare Advantage Plan she can switch to another Medicare Advantage Plan (with or without drug coverage), or drop her plan and return to Original Medicare — and if she returns to Original Medicare she can also join a separate Medicare drug plan. She can only make one change during this period, and the new coverage starts the first of the month after the plan gets her request. (If she returns to Original Medicare and joins a separate drug plan, she doesn't need to contact her Medicare Advantage Plan to disenroll — that happens automatically when she joins the drug plan.) Separately, if something like a move or loss of other coverage happens, a Special Enrollment Period may let her join, switch, or drop a plan at other times.

answer.answer: Possibly, yes — it depends on the plan. Under a Medicare Advantage Plan (also called "Part C"), you may need to get approval from the plan before it covers certain services or drugs (this is called prior authorization), and in some cases you may also need a referral to see a specialist. In many cases you also have to use providers in the plan's network, though some plans cover non-emergency care out of network at a higher cost. Medicare Advantage Plans provide almost all medically necessary services Original Medicare covers, but the rules for getting them differ by plan, so check with the specific plan before joining — including whether her cardiologist is in the network. If she isn't sure whether a service is covered, the handbook says to check with her provider before she gets the service, and she can file an appeal if she disagrees with a coverage decision.

answer.question: Mom is down to two Medicare Advantage plans, an HMO and a PPO. Would she have to pick a primary care doctor or get referrals, and what happens if she sees a doctor outside the network?
answer.answer:
The excerpts answer this for HMO plans but not fully for PPO plans.

With an HMO Plan: in most cases she would need to choose a primary care doctor, and in most cases she'd need a referral to see a specialist — though certain services, like yearly mammogram screenings, don't require a referral. She must generally get care from doctors, other providers, or hospitals in the plan's network, except for emergency care, out-of-area urgent care, or temporary out-of-area dialysis. If she gets non-emergency care outside the network without authorization, she may have to pay the full cost. Some HMOs, called HMO Point-of-Service (HMOPOS) Plans, may let her get some out-of-network services for a higher copayment or coinsurance.

The excerpts here don't give the PPO details (the handbook covers PPO Plans on page 68, which isn't included). In general, the handbook says that with Medicare Advantage Plans you'll often need to use providers in the plan's network, some plans offer non-emergency coverage out of network but at a higher cost, and in some cases you may need a referral to use a specialist or prior authorization for certain services or drugs. For the PPO specifics, check with the plan or visit Medicare.gov — and she can also compare both plans' rules before choosing.

answer.question: Dad has had a Medigap policy for years but wants to try a Medicare Advantage plan. If he hates it, can he get his Medigap policy back?
answer.answer:
Maybe — it depends on whether this is his first Medicare Advantage Plan and whether the insurer still sells the policy.

If he drops his Medigap policy (Medicare Supplement Insurance, which fills "gaps" in Original Medicare) to join a Medicare Advantage Plan for the first time, he gets a single 12-month period — called his "trial right period" — to get his Medigap policy back if the same insurance company still sells it once he returns to Original Medicare. If it isn't available, he can buy certain Medigap policies, depending on state law and whether he's new to Medicare on or after January 1.

Outside that trial right period, he may not be able to get the same policy back, or in some cases any Medigap policy, and he might have to pay more, depending on his state's Medigap enrollment rules and his situation.

Two other practical points: most Medigap policies don't cancel automatically when he joins a Medicare Advantage Plan, so he must contact his insurance company if he wants to cancel it; and Medigap can't be used to pay his Medicare Advantage Plan copayments, deductibles, and premiums. To return to Original Medicare, he can drop the Medicare Advantage Plan during the Medicare Advantage Open Enrollment Period, January 1 to March 31, with coverage starting the first of the month after the plan gets his request. For more details on dropping Medigap, see Medicare.gov/health-drug-plans/medigap/ready-to-buy/change-policies.
